selectedConcepts.concept: Connect the study of medicines and disease with health behaviour, patient experience and public health. Use epidemiology, health psychology and evidence reviews to explore treatment decisions, and examine how communication, access and public policy shape them.

selectedConcepts.labelRationale: Pharmacology, physiology and disease establish the biomedical context. Health psychology, epidemiology and public economics address decisions, access and the social context of care.
selectedConcepts.distinctnessRationale: The options differ by 12 courses and 90 EC each way. The biomedical option emphasises cell biology, biochemistry, laboratory work, immunity and quantitative modelling. The medicine-use option emphasises psychology, qualitative inquiry, communication and public economics.

audience.programmeDescription: Pharmacy at Groningen studies how medicines are developed, how they act in the body and how they are used in patient care. The comparison follows the Pharmacy major.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on the biology of drug action or on how people and health systems make treatment decisions. Groningen also teaches the preparation and analysis of medicines and pharmaceutical care.

cellNotes.text: Both study the functions and regulation of human organ systems.
Both study cells, membranes and molecular processes. Groningen continues the sequence in a second course.
Both study drug targets and receptor mechanisms. UCR Pharmacology also introduces pharmacokinetics and therapeutic examples.
Both study mechanisms of disease across human organ systems.
Both examine immune mechanisms and inflammation. Groningen studies these mechanisms in relation to medicines.
Both develop practical biological laboratory skills. UCR also covers microbiology and protein work.
Both use statistical inference to interpret empirical results. UCR emphasises experimental design and behavioural research.
Both use population study designs and examine bias and risk. Groningen applies these methods to the use and effects of medicines.
Groningen introduces pharmaceutical dosage forms and their behaviour in the body.
Groningen continues formulation and biopharmacy in a second course.
Groningen develops pharmacotherapy and pharmaceutical-care skills.
Groningen devotes a full course to pharmacokinetics. UCR introduces kinetics within Pharmacology.
Groningen reserves 15 EC for three Pharmacy electives.
Groningen requires a 15 EC pharmaceutical research project. The optional UCR research element is separate from the scheduled courses.
Groningen studies how molecular properties affect a substance’s potential as a medicine.
Groningen develops laboratory methods for analysing pharmaceutical substances.
This course includes the Groningen certificate in safe microbiological techniques.

notes.text: The Groningen major combines drug science with pharmaceutical care and professional practice. The UCR options explore biomedical drug mechanisms or the social and behavioural context of medicine use.

UCR Pharmacology introduces drug action and pharmacokinetics. The UCR options lack Groningen’s specialist courses in drug formulation, pharmaceutical analysis and medicinal chemistry, as well as its training in pharmacy practice.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.text: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD112.name: Leadership Communication
BENLEAD112.text: Studies leadership communication through theory, persuasion, emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Students analyse literary characters, film and speeches, interview a leader, prepare a communication advisory report, and develop an address explaining their own ethical leadership vision.

source.reviewNote: Read actual selected current profile; remove confidence/comprehensive-mastery promises and represent concrete methods, projects and limitations proportionately.

BENLEAD211.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
BENLEAD211.text: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.text: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.text: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.text: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.text: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

DISMATH314.text: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

GOSSOCI111.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

GOSSOCI212.text: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

HCBBIOM111.text: Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.

HCBBIOM211.name: Functional Anatomy
HCBBIOM211.text: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Medical images, anatomical drawing, human-specimen material and guided practicals develop spatial reasoning, including observation in a dissection room. Historical, ethical and societal questions accompany these academic learning activities, which do not provide clinical qualification.

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.text: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.

HCBBIOM312.name: Infection & Immunity
HCBBIOM312.text: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.

HCBBIOM313.name: Mechanisms of Disease
HCBBIOM313.text: Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. Students connect anatomy and physiology with symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Clinical cases and an imaginary-disease assignment develop coherent pathophysiological explanations.

HCBCOGN112.name: Neurobiology
HCBCOGN112.text: Neurobiology studies nervous systems and behaviour through comparative anatomy, evolution and physiology. Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.

HCBCOGN311.text: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. Topics include attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.

HCBGATE101.text: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Topics include biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, metabolism, cell division, heredity, gene expression and biotechnology. Students analyse scientific experiments and papers through teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium, with additional topics selected with the class.

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.text: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

HCBPSYC311.name: Medical & Health Psychology

HCBPSYC313.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
HCBPSYC313.text: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. HCBPSYC314.text: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication

Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication.
